edition.deck: Also: a deadly school collapse in Pakistan, an Israeli halt to commercial goods entering Gaza, and fresh findings on investigations into alleged civilian harm.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise developments with immediate human consequences and significant political or security implications. Returning coverage earns space where this gather adds a material development or fresh evidence; lighter or less consequential items are left out.

content.headline: Ukraine resumes strikes as Russia attacks energy sites and Black Sea ships
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine resumes strikes as Russia attacks energy sites
content.standfirst: Kyiv says a pause in attacks on Russian energy infrastructure is over after a major Russian drone barrage. Meanwhile, attacks on commercial ships near Romania’s coast leave sailors missing and raise fears of a wider Black Sea escalation.

image.caption: Rescue teams search rough seas near the burning tanker off Romania’s coast.

sources.originalTitle: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
- Alle alarmklokker bør ringe lige nu, siger sikkerhedspolitisk analytiker

segments.body: Ukraine says it will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after a three-day pause, which President Volodymyr Zelensky says was not matched by Moscow. Russia accused Ukraine of attacking a refinery in Ryazan; it said debris from intercepted missiles and drones caused a fire there. The US-proposed energy ceasefire was never accepted by Russia, according to the reporting.

segments.title: A widening threat at sea
segments.body: Seven crew members are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania. Romanian authorities say two tankers were struck; Russia says it hit two cargo ships carrying military supplies to Ukraine, without naming them. Romania and Bulgaria are discussing whether to seek Nato consultations over the incidents.

segments.title: Ukraine’s reliance on US systems
segments.body: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing was withdrawn to pressure Kyiv to stop attacks, and that restrictions on satellite services disrupted Ukrainian military operations. Some Starlink functions reportedly resumed, but the cause and extent of the restrictions remain unclear. Security analyst Jacob Kaarsbo says European allies could replace some US intelligence support, but sees Ukraine’s reliance on Starlink and Starshield as a more serious vulnerability.

perspectives.body: Kaarsbo argues that European allies could take over much of the intelligence work supplied by the US, but says Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink and Starshield is the greater strategic weakness.

content.headline: At least 33 pupils and a teacher killed in Pakistan school collapse
content.shortHeadline: At least 33 pupils and a teacher die in Pakistan school collapse
content.standfirst: The roof of a classroom at a private school in Peshawar collapsed after lessons began, trapping children beneath the rubble. Officials say the building may have been structurally unsafe; an investigation is under way.

image.caption: Rescue workers and residents search the rubble after the school roof collapsed in Peshawar.

sources.originalTitle: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
Skoletag kollapser og dræber over 30 børn i Pakistan

segments.body: At least 33 pupils and a teacher were killed when a school roof collapsed in Peshawar, in north-west Pakistan, according to hospital officials cited by the BBC. More than a dozen people were injured, some critically. Rescue teams worked in difficult conditions to reach classrooms where children were trapped beneath the debris.

segments.title: Questions over the building
segments.body: Police say the school had substandard roof slabs and was overloaded; the owner has been arrested and an inquiry will examine possible building-code violations. A provincial safety audit of schools has also been ordered. Reports differ on the death toll: the BBC reported 33 pupils and a teacher, while other outlets cited by DR gave totals ranging from 28 to at least 34 children.

content.headline: Hundreds of Israeli military investigations into alleged harm have no publicout
content.shortHeadline: 254 Israeli military investigations have no public outcome
content.standfirst: A BBC Verify review found that the Israeli military said it was examining 300 incidents of alleged harm; only 28 had a published outcome. The findings cover incidents across Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and Israel between 2023 and 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds

segments.body: BBC Verify identified 300 incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces said it was investigating allegations of people killed or injured. It found public outcomes for 28 cases, while the status of 18 more was unclear. At least 254 incidents had no public outcome on the IDF website, including cases dating back to 2023.

segments.title: Calls for transparency, and the IDF’s response
segments.body: The IDF says it publishes findings when possible, subject to legal, operational, privacy and security considerations. International-law experts cited by BBC Verify say investigations should be prompt, thorough and impartial; one former IDF lawyer also points to the difficulties of gathering evidence in combat zones. The IDF did not provide a status breakdown of the cases when asked by the BBC.

content.headline: Israel halts commercial imports into Gaza, leaving aid groups concerned
content.shortHeadline: Israel halts commercial goods entering Gaza
content.standfirst: Israel’s military body overseeing Gaza says it has stopped commercial goods entering the territory. A Norwegian Refugee Council spokesperson warns the move will affect food and other supplies; a Gaza truck association disputes Israel’s stated rationale.

sources.originalTitle: Israel lukker for import af kommercielle varer til Gaza

segments.body: Israel has stopped commercial goods entering Gaza, according to Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry unit that oversees affairs in the territory. The Norwegian Refugee Council says the decision will quickly affect supplies of food and other essentials, and that humanitarian agencies cannot meet the need alone.

Cogat says the decision followed complaints that Hamas was charging fees on trucks bringing in goods. The head of Gaza’s private truck association rejects that claim. The gather does not establish how long the halt will last or what alternative supply arrangements, if any, will be made.

content.headline: Floods kill at least four in Greece and Turkey after torrential rain
content.shortHeadline: At least four dead as floods hit Greece and Turkey
content.standfirst: Flooding has disrupted daily life in Istanbul and on the Greek islands of Rhodes and Evia. Schools have closed in affected areas, while authorities report deaths, missing people and widespread emergency calls.

image.caption: Cars swept away by floodwaters on the Greek island of Rhodes.

sources.originalTitle: Mindst fire personer er omkommet efter oversvømmelser i Grækenland og Tyrkiet

segments.body: At least four people have died in flooding after heavy rain hit parts of Greece and Turkey, according to the report. Istanbul and the Greek islands of Rhodes and Evia were among the hardest-hit areas. Schools in Istanbul and Rhodes were closed, and officials urged people to avoid unnecessary journeys.

segments.title: Rescue work and damage
segments.body: Rhodes received more than 260mm of rain over roughly a day, while parts of Istanbul saw more than 100mm in 12 hours. Authorities on Rhodes reported rescue operations and declared an emergency. In Istanbul, three people were reported dead and four missing; the report also describes one death on Rhodes.

content.headline: Drought in Afghanistan pushes families to marry off young daughters
content.shortHeadline: Afghan families marry off girls as drought deepens poverty
content.standfirst: Families in Badghis say failed harvests and lost livestock have left them in debt and unable to feed their children. Reporting from the province documents girls as young as two being engaged, with aid and health services also under pressure.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides

segments.body: Families displaced by repeated drought in Afghanistan’s Badghis province describe marrying or engaging their daughters to repay debts, pay for food or meet medical costs. The Guardian reports cases involving girls as young as two, and interviews families who say they felt they had no other way to survive.

segments.title: A crisis with lasting consequences
segments.body: The reporting describes girls facing early pregnancy, loss of schooling and risk of violence in their husbands’ households. It also documents families struggling to reach healthcare and humanitarian support. Aid workers warn that clinics treating young brides are disappearing as foreign assistance falls; the extent of the practice across the country is not established by this report.

content.headline: Backlash against US data centres emerges as an issue in midterm races
content.shortHeadline: Data centre backlash enters US midterm races
content.standfirst: Residents across the US are organising against large data centre projects, citing concerns over land, water, energy and noise. Politicians in both parties are responding as the issue begins to shape campaign positions.

image.caption: Residents in Arizona discuss the expansion of data centres near their homes.

sources.originalTitle: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections

segments.body: Opposition to data centre development has spread across US communities and become a concern for politicians preparing for the midterm elections. The BBC reports that the number of local groups opposing projects more than doubled to 833 in the first months of this year, according to Data Center Watch.

segments.title: Local costs and political calculations
segments.body: Residents interviewed by the BBC raised concerns about the scale of projects and demands on local water, energy and air quality. Industry supporters point to jobs, but research cited in the report estimates a new data centre creates around 100 to 200 local jobs. Some politicians have backed pauses or limits, though many such measures are temporary.

content.headline: Neanderthal shoulder wound may be evidence of a fatal spear strike
content.shortHeadline: Neanderthal wound may show a fatal spear strike
content.standfirst: Researchers say a hole in a Neanderthal’s shoulder blade, found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, is consistent with a wooden spear wound more than 70,000 years old. They cannot tell whether it was an attack or an accident.

image.caption: A hole and fractures in the Neanderthal shoulder blade are consistent with a spear wound.

sources.originalTitle: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

segments.body: A Neanderthal skeleton from Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan bears a 1.5cm hole in the shoulder blade, with fractures that researchers say are consistent with a wooden spear striking from the front. The adult, estimated to have died more than 70,000 years ago, may represent the oldest evidence yet of a human ancestor killed by a spear.

The researchers say the wound was probably lethal, but cannot determine whether it resulted from violence or a hunting accident. Other remains at the site suggest Neanderthals returned to bury their dead in the same area over years or decades. The findings are published in Scientific Reports.

content.headline: Reform leader defends vetting after candidates filmed making racist remarks
content.shortHeadline: Farage defends Reform vetting after racist remarks emerge
content.standfirst: Nigel Farage says the party cannot predict what candidates will say after they are selected. ITV’s undercover investigation recorded racist and violent comments; Reform says those filmed are under investigation and several have left or been suspended.

sources.originalTitle: Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments

segments.body: Nigel Farage has defended Reform UK’s candidate-vetting process after ITV broadcast footage of party councillors and candidates making racist, violent and sexist comments. He said the party vets candidates to a higher standard than others, but that it cannot vet for future remarks.

segments.title: Party response and criticism
segments.body: Reform says those filmed are under investigation and have resigned or been suspended. Farage said the most serious comments were unacceptable, while arguing that undercover reporters could find offensive remarks in other parties too. Political opponents have criticised Reform and called for firm action.

content.headline: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sex offences
content.shortHeadline: Jeffrey Donaldson jailed for 15 years for child sex offences
content.standfirst: The former Democratic Unionist Party leader was convicted of 18 offences against two women when they were children. He is seeking to appeal; his wife was found to have committed acts of aiding and abetting, with a decision on her case still pending.

image.caption: Jeffrey Donaldson was returned to Maghaberry prison after sentencing.

sources.originalTitle: Former DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex abuse
Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sexual offences

segments.body: Jeffrey Donaldson, 63, has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex offences against two women, including rape. A judge imposed consecutive terms of 11 years and four years, and ordered that Donaldson remain on the sex offenders’ register for life. He was returned to prison after sentencing.

segments.title: Victims speak and appeal planned
segments.body: The judge said the offending was prolonged and that Donaldson had shown no remorse. The victims described lasting effects in statements read in court. Donaldson denies the offences and is seeking to appeal his convictions. His wife, Eleanor, was found to have committed acts including aiding and abetting; she has applied to appeal that finding, and a further decision on her case is due later.

content.headline: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run low
content.shortHeadline: Severe drought declared across six English areas
content.standfirst: Reservoirs in parts of south-west and south-east England are critically low after the driest April-to-September period in more than a century. Water companies want wider restrictions on business water use, but ministers have not approved them.

image.caption: Ardingly reservoir, which supplies around 95,000 properties, is 19% full.

sources.originalTitle: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run low

segments.body: Six areas—Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex—have been declared in severe drought. Ardingly reservoir is 19% full and Wimbleball is 16%, compared with an expected storage level of about 75% at this point in the year, according to the Environment Agency.

segments.title: Restrictions and monitoring
segments.body: Three water companies have asked to extend restrictions to businesses including golf clubs, private schools and commercial car washes; the environment secretary has not approved the requests. The government and Environment Agency will monitor water and river levels daily and increase water-quality checks as lower river flows could raise pollution risks.

content.headline: Nandy opens way to deeper scrutiny of Sky’s £1.6bn ITV deal
content.shortHeadline: Sky’s £1.6bn ITV deal faces possible media-plurality inquiry
content.standfirst: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is minded to intervene in Sky’s proposed purchase of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm. The companies have five days to respond before she decides whether to trigger formal investigations.

image.caption: Sky has agreed to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm.

sources.originalTitle: Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV

segments.body: Lisa Nandy says she is minded to intervene in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm. Her decision raises public-interest questions about free expression, the range of views in news media and the diversity of media ownership. The companies have five days to respond.

If Nandy proceeds, Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority would conduct formal investigations. Sky, owned by Comcast, says the deal would create a UK-focused streaming business able to compete with global platforms. The gather does not establish whether the takeover will ultimately be blocked.

content.headline: Russell Brand accuser describes alleged rape as trial hears her police interview
content.shortHeadline: Russell Brand accuser gives evidence of alleged 1999 rape
content.standfirst: Jurors heard video of a woman describing an alleged attack in a hotel room after meeting Brand at the 1999 Labour Party conference. Brand denies all charges and has pleaded not guilty; the trial is continuing.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court during his trial.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand told woman ‘it’s just fun’ as he raped her, court hears
Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
Russell Brand was ‘ruthless sexual predator’ – five key takeaways from trial so far

segments.body: A woman told police that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in 1999, the jury at Southwark Crown Court heard through video evidence. She said she had met him at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth and had invited him to continue their conversation in her room.

segments.title: Charges and denial
segments.body: Brand faces seven charges relating to six women: three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault, covering allegations from 1999 to 2009. He denies all charges and says any sexual contact, if it occurred, was consensual. The trial is expected to last six weeks.

content.headline: HSE finds safety breaches at more than half of inspected quartz-worktop firms
content.shortHeadline: More than half of inspected quartz-worktop firms breached safety rules
content.standfirst: Inspectors found breaches at 56% of 434 engineered-stone workshops, including 47 cases serious enough for a ban on work. Workers exposed to silica dust can develop silicosis, an incurable lung disease; the HSE plans to inspect 1,000 firms.

image.caption: The HSE has inspected more than 400 firms that cut engineered-stone worktops.

sources.originalTitle: Revealed: The human cost of UK’s killer kitchens – with 166 firms breaking law
Kitchen refit worker, 32, dies of lung disease after calling for deadly stone ban

segments.body: The Health and Safety Executive found safety breaches at 56% of 434 quartz-worktop businesses inspected since May. It issued legally binding notices to 166 firms, including 47 prohibition notices that immediately stop a work activity because of serious risk. In one case, inspectors found dust billowing from a workshop as workers cut stone.

segments.title: Health risks and enforcement
segments.body: Dry cutting engineered stone can release respirable crystalline silica, which causes silicosis. The i Paper reports that nearly 60 UK stonemasons have been diagnosed, while doctors fear the true number is higher. A separate report on the death of worker Malik Al-Khalil describes the disease’s severe effects and a coroner’s concerns about workplace exposure.

content.headline: Argentina’s president shares adviser’s claim that UK is being ‘colonised byIslam
content.shortHeadline: Milei shares adviser’s claim that UK is being ‘colonised by Islam’
content.standfirst: Javier Milei shared a post by adviser Santiago Caputo linking the election of a Muslim British MP to Argentina’s claim on the Falkland Islands. The comments come amid renewed tensions over the territory and its emerging oil industry.

image.caption: A Union flag flies outside a property in Stanley, the Falkland Islands’ capital.

sources.originalTitle: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows

segments.body: Santiago Caputo, a senior adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, invoked the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as a British MP to argue that Argentina should reclaim the Falkland Islands. Milei shared the post, which described Britain as being “colonised by Islam” and framed the islands as a strategic issue for the West.

segments.title: A long-running sovereignty dispute
segments.body: The comments come amid heightened tensions between Argentina and the UK over the islands and their developing oil industry. The Guardian reports that UK officials have sought assurances from Interpol over possible requests to detain people working there. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of islanders voted to remain a British territory.

content.headline: MI5 warns AI could help terrorists develop biological weapons
content.shortHeadline: MI5 chief warns AI could help terrorists develop bioweapons
content.standfirst: MI5 director general Ken McCallum says AI could put dangerous biological knowledge within reach of less sophisticated actors. The agency has launched a centre to assess AI-related security risks; the threat remains a possibility, not a reported attack.

image.caption: MI5’s director general has warned that AI could increase security risks.

sources.originalTitle: UK at growing risk of terror attack with deadly man-made viruses, warns MI5 boss

segments.body: MI5 chief Ken McCallum warned that artificial intelligence could make it easier for terrorists to obtain knowledge needed to develop biological weapons. He said the risk had not yet materialised, but could give comparatively low-sophistication actors new capabilities. MI5 has launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre to examine risks and opportunities.

segments.title: A wider security warning
segments.body: McCallum also described Russia as the UK’s leading state threat and said Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the UK over the past year. He warned against overstating Russian online influence, saying that keeping public attention fixed on trolls could amplify their effect.

content.headline: Eight-year-old injured after falling from Bakken ride; investigation under way
content.shortHeadline: Girl injured after falling from Bakken ride
content.standfirst: The girl remains in hospital with injuries requiring treatment but is not in life-threatening condition. The ride has been taken out of service while police and its owner investigate how she fell.

image.caption: The Polyppen ride at Bakken, shown in an archive image.

sources.originalTitle: Pige røg ud af forlystelse på Bakken – forlystelsesparken reagerer
Otteårig indlagt efter fald fra forlystelse på Bakken

segments.body: An eight-year-old girl fell from the Polyppen ride at the Bakken amusement park near Copenhagen on Wednesday. Police say she remains in hospital with injuries requiring treatment but is not in life-threatening condition. The ride has been closed while the incident is investigated.

Bakken says the ride’s owner is working with the authorities to establish what happened. Police say the incident could lead to criminal liability if a fault with the ride is found. The cause has not been established.

content.headline: Man dies as storm brings 60m/s gusts and damage across the Faroe Islands
content.shortHeadline: One dead as storm hits the Faroe Islands
content.standfirst: A storm brought gusts of up to 60 metres per second, flooding and more than 50 reports of damage to buildings across the islands. Authorities say the unusually long spell of strong winds lasted about a day.

image.caption: Storm clouds over Toftir and Skálafjørður in the Faroe Islands on Wednesday.

sources.originalTitle: Mand dræbt under storm i Færøerne og over 50 skader på huse og udhuse

segments.body: A man died on Suðuroy after being struck by a flying object during a storm in the Faroe Islands, police say. More than 50 buildings were damaged, while heavy rain caused flooding and landslides that blocked roads. Ferry and bus services were cancelled and police urged people to stay indoors.

Gusts reached up to 60 metres per second, according to police. The storm lasted around 24 hours, which authorities described as unusual, although powerful winds are not uncommon in the Faroes. Conditions were easing by Thursday afternoon.

content.headline: Supreme Court rules AI-generated sexual images of children are illegal
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s Supreme Court rules AI child-abuse images are illegal
content.standfirst: The court upheld an 18-month prison sentence for a man who admitted creating and sharing 36,209 AI-generated images depicting sexual material involving minors. The ruling establishes that fictional images are covered by the law.

sources.originalTitle: "Retshistorie" – Højesteret stadfæster dom i sag om AI-genereret seksuelt materiale med børn

segments.body: Denmark’s Supreme Court has upheld an 18-month prison sentence for a man who admitted creating and distributing 36,209 AI-generated images depicting sexual material involving people under 18. The court ruled that the images are covered by the law even if the depicted people are fictional.

segments.title: A first for the top court
segments.body: The case is the first of its kind to reach Denmark’s Supreme Court. The defendant argued that no real child was harmed and said he believed the images reduced the amount of real abuse material in circulation. The court rejected that distinction; his defence says he is disappointed by the ruling.

perspectives.body: The defence says its client believed making fictional images would reduce real abuse material, and is disappointed that the court treated the material under the same law.

content.headline: Report finds violence in more than half of Danish school classes
content.shortHeadline: More than half of Danish school classes report violence
content.standfirst: A new report says more than half of the country’s classes experience violence between pupils during a school year, rising to three-quarters in the youngest grades. The education minister calls the figures too high; experts differ on the response.

sources.originalTitle: Sønnens hovedbund og blå mærker viser stort problem i danske folkeskoler

segments.body: More than half of Danish school classes experience violence between pupils in a school year, according to a new report cited by TV 2. In classes from kindergarten through third grade, the figure is three in four. The report comes alongside a pupil’s account of repeated bullying and physical assaults at his former school.

segments.title: How schools should respond
segments.body: Education Minister Magnus Heunicke called the figures a real problem and argued for more trained teachers and authority to intervene early. Children’s welfare adviser Lone Smidt says physical intervention will not restore a sense of safety and points to pressure on a small number of pupils in some classes. The report’s full findings are not included in the gather.

content.headline: Citizens propose shifting social-benefit costs from Danish municipalities to the
content.shortHeadline: Proposal would shift social-benefit costs to Danish state
content.standfirst: A citizens’ proposal backed by residents of Lolland and Guldborgsund would leave municipalities handling benefit cases but have the state pay the bill. Experts disagree on whether that division could work.

image.caption: Proposal supporter Paw Justin Mistarz presents the “Danmarks-Kassen” idea.

sources.originalTitle: Sociale ydelser skal udelukkende betales af staten, lyder et borgerforslag

segments.body: Five residents have proposed moving the cost of benefits such as social assistance and disability pensions from municipalities to the state. They say poorer municipalities, including Lolland, are under pressure to cut services, while still having to fund benefits for eligible residents.

segments.title: Experts divided on the plan
segments.body: An Aalborg University professor warns that separating casework from funding could lead to serious problems. Another economist says state rules could be attached to municipal administration and argues that the proposal raises a wider issue of how social and care costs are shared. A government committee is reviewing the equalisation system, with changes expected in 2029.

perspectives.body: The report presents contrasting views: one economist warns that municipalities administering benefits funded by the state could create problems; another says state rules could make the arrangement workable.

content.headline: Haddock stocks reach a record high, but researchers expect a decline
content.shortHeadline: Haddock stocks hit record high as fishers see a strong catch
content.standfirst: Fishers landed almost three times as much haddock in September as a year earlier, and DTU Aqua says stocks are at their highest since assessments began in 1972. Researchers expect the population to fall from this high level in coming years.

image.caption: Freshly landed haddock at a Danish fishing port.

sources.originalTitle: Vestjysk havneby svømmer i kuller - bestanden er historisk høj

segments.body: Haddock landings in September reached 240 tonnes, nearly three times the level a year earlier. The fish are also fetching a higher price, offering a welcome catch for fishers in a sector exposed to changing quotas, weather and markets. DTU Aqua says the stock has reached a record level in its assessments.

segments.title: A high point may not last
segments.body: Researchers attribute the increase to several strong year groups of young haddock and lower fishing pressure. They say the stock is not expected to keep growing: no similarly strong year group has appeared since 2022, so numbers may fall over the next few years, although from a high level.

content.headline: Man, 81, admits violence causing death after fatal Odense stabbing
content.shortHeadline: 81-year-old admits fatal violence but denies intent to kill
content.standfirst: The 81-year-old says he was angry with his 65-year-old downstairs neighbour before stabbing him in Odense. He admits violence resulting in death but denies intending to kill; a judge has remanded him in custody in a psychiatric facility.

image.caption: Police at the scene on Nedergade in central Odense on Wednesday morning.

sources.originalTitle: 81-årig forklarer knivdrab – var "megasur" på underbo

segments.body: An 81-year-old man has admitted violence resulting in death after his 65-year-old neighbour was stabbed in central Odense on Wednesday. He denies intending to kill him. The defendant has been remanded for four weeks in a psychiatric facility while the case proceeds.

The defendant told a court he was angry with his neighbour, reportedly after a dispute involving a letter. Prosecutors say he stabbed the man several times in the chest and arm. The defendant has agreed to a mental examination; police have not found the alleged weapon, according to the report.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album becomes a bittersweet farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s final album is a farewell to Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says Danceteria will be Soft Cell’s last record after Ball died two days after they finished it. The album looks back to the New York club scene that shaped the duo and their sound.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed their new songs were finished. Two days later, keyboardist Dave Ball died, aged 66. Danceteria, released after his death, is the duo’s sixth and final album: Marc Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell record without him.

segments.title: A closing chapter in New York
segments.body: The album revisits the pair’s early-1980s experiences in New York and its Danceteria nightclub, mixing exuberant dance-pop with songs about loneliness and regret. Almond describes the record as a full-circle ending, and says the two were closer while making it than they had been for some time.

content.headline: The Go-Betweens’ messy history helps explain their enduring appeal
content.shortHeadline: The Go-Betweens’ messy history and enduring appeal
content.standfirst: A new live album and reissues renew attention on the Australian band whose literate, emotionally complicated songs never quite broke through. The story also restores drummer Lindy Morrison and multi-instrumentalist Amanda Brown to the picture.

image.caption: Grant McLennan and Robert Forster of the Go-Betweens in 2000.

sources.originalTitle: The messy, bizarre inside story of The Go-Betweens

segments.body: Robert Forster and Grant McLennan wrote strikingly different songs, but The Go-Betweens never turned their singular mix of literary detail and pop melody into mainstream success. A new 1987 live album, Fountains of Youth, arrives alongside reissues of several records.

segments.title: The people behind the songs
segments.body: The account traces the band’s personal tensions through the making of 16 Lovers Lane, while making clear that Lindy Morrison and Amanda Brown were more than supporting figures in its history. Brown has said that she and Morrison felt erased from the story for years; their contributions, and the band’s complicated legacy, remain part of its renewed attention.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family affair
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello’s solo album turns protest into a family affair
content.standfirst: The Rage Against the Machine guitarist calls Everyone Gets What They Want an answer to the far-right and a record for people who have “had enough”. He also discusses the activism of his mother and writing with his teenage son.

image.caption: Tom Morello, guitarist and founding member of Rage Against the Machine.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as his first full-length solo rock album, with him at the microphone rather than only behind the guitar. He calls it a protest record against racism and fascism, continuing the activism he has brought to Rage Against the Machine and other projects.

segments.title: An inheritance of activism
segments.body: Morello says his mother, Mary, instilled in him the idea that ordinary people can change the world. She joined causes ranging from workers’ rights to anti-racism; his son Roman, 15, co-wrote five tracks on the album. Morello also addresses criticism from some older fans who object to his political views.

content.headline: Richard Thompson on wild crowds, Sandy Denny and almost joining the Eagles
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson on wild crowds and almost joining the Eagles
content.standfirst: The folk guitarist answers readers’ questions as he releases Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, recalling his musical contemporaries, a knife-wielding audience member in Sweden and why he stayed on his own path.

image.caption: Richard Thompson, whose new album is Hippies, Thugs and Heroes.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills

segments.body: Richard Thompson looks back on a career spent among musicians including Sandy Denny, Nick Drake and John Martyn. He says the folk scene’s artists felt different rather than special, and recalls how a neighbour’s motorcycle helped inspire “1952 Vincent Black Lightning”.

segments.title: A musician on his own terms
segments.body: Thompson says he turned down a firm approach to join Linda Ronstadt’s band while touring with Denny, before the musicians who left Ronstadt went on to form the Eagles. He also recounts a Swedish show where a man held a knife to his throat and demanded “something normal”, and describes the uneasy, fictional territory songwriters can explore.

content.headline: The Mary Wallopers turn grisly folk stories into a rowdy live party
content.shortHeadline: The Mary Wallopers make folk a rowdy live party
content.standfirst: The Irish six-piece mix fast, politically pointed songs with quieter, more serious performances on their biggest tour yet. At Edinburgh’s Corn Exchange, the crowd’s energy becomes part of the show.

image.caption: Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers performing live.

sources.originalTitle: The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragers

segments.body: The Mary Wallopers send a crowd surging to a song about an early-18th-century killer-for-hire, then turn from rowdy singalongs to a sparse performance of “Smuggling the Tin”. The band’s live show makes old stories feel immediate without sanding away their rough edges.

segments.title: Tradition with a sharp edge
segments.body: Songs on the tour’s accompanying album, Paddywhackery, pair humour with politics, taking aim at capitalism and British rule while confronting criticism that the band is “too Irish”. The review finds the group’s shifts between high-energy revelry and stillness central to its case for folk’s continued relevance.

content.headline: Angèle’s new album brings bold Francophone pop to a wider audience
content.shortHeadline: Angèle’s bold new album tests pop’s language barrier
content.standfirst: The Belgian star works with Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek on Instinct, an album that veers from familiar pop to noisy, unpredictable turns. The review finds its best moments exciting but its overall effect uneven.

image.caption: Belgian singer Angèle.

sources.originalTitle: Angèle: Instinct review – Belgium’s biggest star is determined to do pop differently

segments.body: Angèle is a major star among Francophone listeners, but has yet to make a comparable impression in Britain. Instinct adds more English lyrics and high-profile collaborators, including Justice and Soulwax, without abandoning the French-language pop that has defined her work.

segments.title: Pop that swerves off course
segments.body: The review praises tracks that suddenly break from their expected shape: piano ballad “On Verra” is interrupted by static and rapid-fire noise, while “Love Triangle” builds around an abrasive synth line. More conventional songs make the album frustrating as well as adventurous, and the review concludes that it is stronger for cherry-picking than for repeated full-album listens.

content.headline: Fontaines D.C.’s Dopamine Chamber makes disillusionment seductive
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C. turn disillusionment into seductive pop
content.standfirst: Pitchfork hears a sleek, expansive record that draws listeners into beautiful escape before leaving them with a portrait of pleasure, loneliness and emotional numbness.

sources.originalTitle: Dopamine Chamber

segments.body: Dopamine Chamber pairs Fontaines D.C.’s large-scale rock sound with a darker idea: that people can be so accustomed to chasing pleasure that they struggle to feel much at all. The review describes the music as seductive rather than simply angry, using beauty to draw listeners into its unease.

segments.title: The lure of escape
segments.body: Grian Chatten’s lyrics adopt the voice of a tempting, sometimes sinister guide, offering disappearance and desire against polished, expansive arrangements. The review singles out “Where Is Gone?”, where Rosalía and Chatten trade lines, as both beautiful and chilling.

content.headline: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3 finds Harlem rapper Errol Holden in vivid detail
content.shortHeadline: Errol Holden’s Harlem vignettes shine on SUPREME MAGNETIC 3
content.standfirst: Pitchfork praises the rapper’s dense, autobiographical verses and ominous production, which turn small details of New York life and memory into an absorbing portrait.

sources.originalTitle: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3

segments.body: On SUPREME MAGNETIC 3, Harlem rapper Errol Holden builds a personal history out of sharply observed fragments: vanished storefronts, family memories and details of street life. Pitchfork finds his writing vivid without unnecessary ornament, delivered at a pace that makes the record feel restless and alive.

segments.title: Space for the stories
segments.body: The production, largely by returning collaborator 2000 Souls, shifts between eerie loops, piano and spacious beats that leave room for Holden’s rapid, intricate flows. The review sees the album as a compelling addition to his catalogue and values its attention to personal detail in a musical landscape it describes as increasingly prone to shortcuts.

content.headline: London’s Prince Charles Cinema secures a 25-year lease
content.shortHeadline: Prince Charles Cinema secures its future with 25-year lease
content.standfirst: The Leicester Square repertory venue says its new agreement has no break clause, ending 21 months of uncertainty. Its owner says the security will allow the cinema to invest in its next chapter.

image.caption: The Prince Charles Cinema in London’s Leicester Square.

sources.originalTitle: Cult venue Prince Charles cinema ‘saved’ after lease renewal signed

segments.body: The Prince Charles Cinema has signed a new 25-year lease with its landlords, securing the future of the central London repertory venue. The cinema said the agreement has no break clause, after a lengthy dispute over a proposed provision that could have allowed the landlord to give six months’ notice.

segments.title: A community-backed reprieve
segments.body: The cinema’s campaign against the break clause drew support from film fans and industry figures, and Westminster City Council designated the building an asset of community value in 2025. The landlord’s chief executive also welcomed the new agreement, saying the company plans to develop a hotel on the building’s upper floors.

content.headline: Lance Oppenheim’s two films probe the blurred line between reality and show
content.shortHeadline: Lance Oppenheim on two films that bend reality
content.standfirst: The director discusses Primetime, with Robert Pattinson as TV host Chris Hansen, and documentary You Can See Everything, made with Nathan Fielder. Both projects ask how performance shapes our sense of truth.

image.caption: Lance Oppenheim, director of Primetime and You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest films

segments.body: Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime turns the confrontational television format of To Catch a Predator into a fictional feature starring Robert Pattinson as host Chris Hansen. Oppenheim says the source material’s strange blend of crime reporting, moral certainty and entertainment made it difficult to adapt without making the result stranger still.

segments.title: The performance behind the persona
segments.body: Oppenheim sees Hansen as both a journalist and an entertainer, a figure whose righteous-avenger image sits uneasily beside his work as a media personality. In You Can See Everything, co-directed with Nathan Fielder, the filmmakers follow Elizabeth Holmes before she enters prison; Oppenheim describes the experience of filming her as one of daily “cognitive dissonance”.

content.headline: Rebellion revisits the Bradford 12 and Britain’s racist past
content.shortHeadline: Rebellion revisits the Bradford 12 and Britain’s racist past
content.standfirst: Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood’s documentary recalls the 1981 arrests and acquittals of 12 South Asian anti-racist activists. The Guardian praises its historical context while criticising an omission in its account of solidarity.

image.caption: Some of the Bradford 12 in 1982.

sources.originalTitle: Rebellion review – story of Bradford 12 revisits Britain’s ugly racist past

segments.body: Rebellion tells the story of 12 members of Bradford’s United Black Youth League, arrested in 1981 over petrol-filled bottles and acquitted after arguing they were preparing to defend themselves from racist attacks. The review places the case amid a wider climate of prejudice, state hostility and violence against anti-racist campaigners.

segments.title: A pointed criticism
segments.body: The Guardian praises the film’s wider account of liberationist politics but argues that its treatment of solidarity has a notable gap: it does not name antisemitism, despite including footage of the National Front, which openly targeted Jewish people. The review says the omission matters to the film’s own stated concern with solidarity.

content.headline: Faust review: FW Murnau’s silent film remains a dazzling vision
content.shortHeadline: Murnau’s Faust remains a dazzling silent-film vision
content.standfirst: A century after its release, the German expressionist fantasy still impresses with its visual scale, dark comedy and striking Mephisto. The Guardian revisits its adaptation of Goethe’s tale.

image.caption: Gösta Ekman as Faust in FW Murnau’s 1926 film.

sources.originalTitle: Faust review – FW Murnau’s silent masterpiece is a devilishly dazzling vision

segments.body: FW Murnau’s 1926 Faust retells Goethe’s story of a scholar who bargains with the devil and finds redemption through love. The Guardian describes it as a mysterious, visually ambitious film, distinct from Christopher Marlowe’s more unforgiving version of the tale.

segments.title: A world of shadow and spectacle
segments.body: Gösta Ekman plays Faust, with Emil Jannings as a capering Mephisto. The review highlights the film’s model landscapes and the image of Mephisto looming over a city like a vast dark angel, while noting its blend of Weimar-era energy, satire and black comedy.

content.headline: Whalefall review: a survival thriller struggles to escape its premise
content.shortHeadline: Whalefall’s survival thriller is trapped by its premise
content.standfirst: Austin Abrams is trapped inside a sperm whale in Brian Duffield’s adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s novel. The Guardian finds moments of visceral horror, but says flashbacks and an overlong runtime blunt the tension.

image.caption: Austin Abrams in Whalefall.

sources.originalTitle: Whalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestible

segments.body: Whalefall follows Jay, played by Austin Abrams, after he is swallowed by a sperm whale while searching for his father’s body. The review finds the predicament immediately gripping, with stomach acid and a swallowed squid providing some effective, unpleasant set pieces.

segments.title: A long way to go
segments.body: The film uses flashbacks to explore Jay’s relationship with his father, played by Josh Brolin, but the Guardian says they do little to deepen the stakes. It argues that the 106-minute film becomes weighed down by familiar family drama and repetitive problem-solving, despite the visual force of its underwater setting.

content.headline: Digger review: Tom Cruise takes a strange, politically blunt risk
content.shortHeadline: Digger is Tom Cruise’s strange, politically blunt risk
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire recasts Cruise as a paunchy oil baron facing the consequences of a climate disaster. BBC Culture calls it an excessive, divisive folly—and says that is part of its appeal.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Tom Cruise plays oil billionaire Digger Rockwell in a film that begins with a company drilling operation cracking a glacier, followed by an iceberg threatening cities. The review calls the premise a blunt satire of money, power and climate crisis, made to feel uncomfortably plausible.

segments.title: A deliberate gamble
segments.body: The review sees Cruise’s transformation into an ageing, paunchy oil baron and the film’s loud, hectoring style as a gamble rather than an attempt at conventional prestige. It concedes that some scenes run too long, but praises the scale of Cruise’s performance and the film’s willingness to be strange and politically direct.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning review: a Facebook exposé without enough tension
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning lacks the tension of its Facebook exposé
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel dramatizes journalist Jeff Horwitz and whistleblower Frances Haugen’s reporting on Facebook. BBC Culture says the story matters, but the film’s uneventful drama struggles to make its case land.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, and Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, as they expose the company’s internal research and its effects on users. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in a smaller role than Jesse Eisenberg had in the first film.

segments.title: A case without a reckoning
segments.body: BBC Culture says the film makes its strongest impression when presenting information about social media’s effects on mental health, but finds little danger or conflict for its central characters. It argues that Sorkin’s brisk dialogue cannot make the two timelines cohere, leaving the film without the tension or impact its subject demands.

content.headline: Fourteen film flops that deserve a second look
content.shortHeadline: Fourteen film flops worth rediscovering
content.standfirst: From The Thing and Dune to Cloud Atlas and Babylon, the i Paper argues that box-office failure is not the same as artistic failure. Its selection revisits films whose reputations have changed or remain open to debate.

image.caption: A selection of films once dismissed as flops and later reconsidered.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The list uses the commercial troubles surrounding Digger as a prompt to look back at films that failed on release but later found admirers. Its picks range from Michael Cimino’s Heaven’s Gate and David Lynch’s Dune to The Thing, Last Action Hero and Babylon.

segments.title: Failure is not a verdict
segments.body: The selections make different cases: some films were misunderstood, some were ambitious experiments, and others have attracted new appreciation over time. The list also leaves room for disagreement, treating a poor box office result as an invitation to reassess rather than proof that a film is a classic.

content.headline: The Diplomat returns with nuclear brinkmanship and marital tension
content.shortHeadline: The Diplomat turns up the pressure in its fourth series
content.standfirst: Keri Russell’s ambassador Kate Wyler is again trying to prevent a geopolitical crisis, while her relationship with Hal grows more fraught. The Guardian review relishes the show’s mix of high stakes and sharply observed personal games.

image.caption: Keri Russell as Kate Wyler in The Diplomat.

sources.originalTitle: The Diplomat review – nothing else on TV is as entertaining as this exquisitely stressful show

segments.body: The Diplomat’s fourth series opens with a Russian submarine at the bottom of the North Sea and a nuclear missile in American hands. Kate Wyler warns that Russia may retaliate against the UK, while her husband, Hal, now US vice-president, is reluctant to come clean.

segments.title: Crisis and chemistry
segments.body: The Guardian says the show raises both geopolitical and personal stakes, with Kate caught between a looming catastrophe and the shifting loyalties around her. It finds the small shifts in power and affection between the characters as compelling as the series’ deliberately heightened brinkmanship.

content.headline: The Book That Changed My Life makes a moving case for reading
content.shortHeadline: The Book That Changed My Life celebrates reading’s power
content.standfirst: This BBC documentary follows people who found a way through prison, illiteracy and isolation with books. The Guardian praises its honest, unsentimental stories—and Queen Camilla’s unexpected literary confession.

image.caption: Queen Camilla in The Book That Changed My Life.

sources.originalTitle: The Book That Changed My Life review – these joyful tales of the power of reading are TV magic

segments.body: The Book That Changed My Life gathers stories from people who say reading altered or saved their lives. Omar describes discovering a book while in prison; Peter recalls learning to read as an adult after years of struggling with literacy.

segments.title: A route into other worlds
segments.body: The Guardian finds the documentary’s most affecting moments in its accounts of reading as escape, confidence and connection. Queen Camilla also appears, recalling her love of The Scarlet Pimpernel as a teenager and describing books as something that makes life better.

content.headline: The Split Up gives a British Asian family a new legal-drama stage
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to the fore
content.standfirst: Ritu Arya leads the Manchester-set spin-off, with Sanjeev Bhaskar as her father. Its creators describe a familiar mix of family conflict and courtroom drama, built around a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows a family-run divorce law firm in Manchester, where Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, expects to take over from her father, Dhruv, played by Sanjeev Bhaskar. Her mother’s death disrupts those plans, and a former romantic partner’s arrival adds another complication.

segments.title: Representation and reinvention
segments.body: The spin-off has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to show British Asian characters living ordinary lives, while executive producer Abi Morgan says the series keeps The Split’s focus on family, relationships and betrayal while giving a new team room to shape it.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani on writing The Party and turning class into drama
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on The Party and writing about class
content.standfirst: The actor and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel for ITV, her experience of grief and the changes she has seen in Hollywood since #MeToo.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner of The Party.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: Sarah Solemani writes and stars in The Party, a drama about a working-class journalist and a Conservative politician whose friendship conceals a dark secret. She says she wanted to bring the British class system to the screen through a story of ambition, old connections and a birthday gathering.

segments.title: A creative life shaped by loss
segments.body: Solemani recalls performing monologues beside her mother’s hospice bed at 16, then receiving news of her acceptance to the National Youth Theatre two weeks after her mother died. She also says #MeToo changed Hollywood by removing dangerous men and bringing intimacy supervisors onto sets.

content.headline: Amol Rajan’s first YouTube interview plays it safer than its ambition
content.shortHeadline: Amol Rajan’s YouTube debut is less radical than promised
content.standfirst: Rajan’s first episode of The Amol Rajan Connection features Gareth Southgate, but the Guardian finds a conventional two-hour conversation beneath the bold branding.

image.caption: The Amol Rajan Connection, Rajan’s new YouTube programme.

sources.originalTitle: The Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors?

segments.body: The Amol Rajan Connection launches with Gareth Southgate, ranging from his football career to FIFA, Manchester City and young men’s lives. The Guardian finds much of the discussion engaging, but says the long-form interview feels conventional rather than like a radical new kind of broadcasting.

segments.title: A new platform, familiar questions
segments.body: The review questions Rajan’s claim that independent online video is “where the action is”, noting that his first guest and the format do little to establish a distinctive proposition. It also observes that leaving the BBC has not, in this opening conversation, produced the greater freedom of expression he has suggested seeking.

content.headline: Crystal Lake stretches Friday the 13th into an unnecessary series
content.shortHeadline: Crystal Lake gives Friday the 13th more backstory than it needs
content.standfirst: Linda Cardellini leads an eight-part prequel about Jason Voorhees’s mother. The Guardian says her performance cannot overcome a muddled show that expands a deliberately thin slasher premise.

image.caption: Linda Cardellini in Crystal Lake.

sources.originalTitle: Crystal Lake review – Friday the 13th gets unnecessary expansion in gory and goofy series

segments.body: Crystal Lake turns Friday the 13th’s brief portrait of Pamela Voorhees into an eight-part account of her life and the events around her son Jason. The Guardian sees the premise as an example of franchise expansion for its own sake, layering backstory onto a character previously defined by a plot twist.

segments.title: A strong lead, an overfilled story
segments.body: Linda Cardellini gives the role a committed performance, but the review says the series keeps changing tone as it adds conspiracies, romance and other subplots. Horror fans may find pleasures in its gore and fan service; the Guardian doubts the expanded story offers enough to justify the series.

content.headline: Carrie’s new TV adaptation raises questions about fidelity and casting
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s new adaptation renews debate over casting and fidelity
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s series reimagines Stephen King’s bullied teenager for the social-media era. BBC Culture examines fans’ objections to the casting and character changes, alongside the case for adapting the novel on its own terms.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the Prime Video series.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: The new Carrie series changes the background of King’s bullied, telekinetic teenager, including making her home-schooled before she enters school. Viewers have also questioned why screen versions repeatedly cast conventionally attractive actresses in a role the novel describes very differently.

segments.title: Adaptation and expectation
segments.body: A horror scholar quoted by BBC Culture says the series updates familiar school bullying for social media, while a filmmaker points to the pressures casting choices can face from the market. The article also argues that adaptation need not mean strict fidelity, and praises Flanagan’s version as a layered story for the present.

content.headline: What to watch tonight: Break Clause, The Celebrity Traitors and more
content.shortHeadline: Tonight’s TV: Break Clause, The Celebrity Traitors and more
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s evening guide previews the final double bill of Channel 4’s housing-crisis romcom and the latest Celebrity Traitors, alongside programmes about Britain’s small islands, animal care and Powell and Pressburger.

image.caption: Ben and Lil in Channel 4’s Break Clause.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: can a breakup in a flatshare ever end well?

segments.body: Break Clause reaches its finale with Ben and Lil facing a decision about their relationship and shared flat as the lease break clause approaches. The Celebrity Traitors also continues, with the guide asking whether its remaining Traitors can avoid detection.

segments.title: More for the evening
segments.body: Other choices include a series about small islands around the UK coast, a veterinary programme and a Sky Arts discussion of Powell and Pressburger’s wartime fantasy A Matter of Life and Death. The guide offers a range of viewing rather than a single recommendation.

content.headline: Rainbow Six Tactics takes Ubisoft Paris from Mario to military strategy
content.shortHeadline: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario to Rainbow Six Tactics
content.standfirst: After making Mario + Rabbids, the studio is adapting Rainbow Six Siege into a turn-based tactics game. Its developers explain how they are carrying the series’ planning and teamwork into a different genre.

image.caption: Rainbow Six Tactics, Ubisoft Paris’s turn-based strategy game.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics swaps the colourful world of Mario + Rabbids for military operations, where players plan coordinated assaults before carrying them out. Ubisoft Paris’s developers say the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequential decisions makes it a natural fit for turn-based strategy.

segments.title: Different routes through a mission
segments.body: A demonstration included drone reconnaissance, explosives, smoke and a hostage extraction, with non-lethal arrests offering another way to gather intelligence. The creative director says the game is designed to leave room for experimentation rather than dictate a single solution, using 15 operators with different approaches.

content.headline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is gory, inventive and uneven
content.shortHeadline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a lively but uneven return
content.standfirst: The new entry trades some traditional exploration for fast combat and demanding platforming. The Guardian finds a striking gothic world and clever puzzles, but also frustrating stretches that struggle to sustain momentum.

image.caption: Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.

sources.originalTitle: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

segments.body: In Belmont’s Curse, Rose Belmont fights through a demon-filled Paris and Dracula’s castle. The review praises the hectic combat, difficult boss battles and grotesque spectacle, while noting that the faster, twitch-focused action may disappoint players looking for the series’ older emphasis on exploration and secret-hunting.

segments.title: A striking world with rough patches
segments.body: The game mixes challenge rooms, platforming and puzzles, including an imaginative sequence involving a cursed portrait and a magic organ. The Guardian says the experience improves after an early plot turn, but finds some areas repetitive and the game unable to match its strongest contemporary peers.

content.headline: End of Abyss makes survival horror small, eerie and exhausting
content.shortHeadline: End of Abyss shrinks survival horror to dollhouse scale
content.standfirst: The game’s dollhouse view and carefully composed rooms create striking scares, but confusing controls and repeated backtracking wear down the experience, the Guardian argues.

image.caption: A view of End of Abyss’s miniature, shadowed facility.

sources.originalTitle: End of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing

segments.body: End of Abyss presents an abandoned facility as a miniature world of dark rooms and exposed interiors. The Guardian praises its unsettling contrast of cute proportions and grisly detail, and the way monsters can emerge at the edge of the player’s vision.

segments.title: When the maze wears thin
segments.body: The review says the fixed camera and survival-horror combat can make encounters tense, but the controls are awkward and the facility’s connected layout encourages too much backtracking. Its oppressive visual style also makes rooms difficult to distinguish, eventually draining the force from carefully staged scares.

content.headline: Playing Call of Duty with his son brings a father back to the joy of games
content.shortHeadline: A father and son rediscover the joy of gaming together
content.standfirst: A Guardian writer and his 22-year-old son return to the first game they played together. Their co-op sessions become a story about growing up, finding time and sharing an old bond.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son play together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his adult son revisit Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together when the son was five. They return to missions they never completed, fail repeatedly and gradually find a rhythm that lets one cover enemies from a distance while the other moves in.

segments.title: Time well spent
segments.body: The sessions remind the writer of the uncomplicated pleasure of playing without worrying about progress or productivity. With the pair expecting to move to different parts of the world in a few months, the article becomes a reflection on a temporary stretch of closeness—and on how games can hold a family memory.

content.headline: Roman fort in Wales offers new evidence behind a medieval legend
content.shortHeadline: Roman fort offers new evidence behind Welsh legend
content.standfirst: Fourth-century coins and other finds at a newly identified fort in Pembrokeshire suggest a medieval tale about the emperor Magnus Maximus has a basis in history. They do not establish that he was at the site.

image.caption: A mock-up of the Roman site in the Preseli Hills, Pembrokeshire.

sources.originalTitle: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

segments.body: Archaeologists have found a fortified Roman site near Frenni Fawr in Pembrokeshire, close to the place where a medieval Welsh tale says the fourth-century emperor Magnus Maximus camped. Coins dating to the late fourth century, Roman tiles, pottery and other finds support the possibility that the story has a historical basis.

segments.title: What the excavation reveals
segments.body: The fort measures about 180 by 150 metres and may have housed around 500 troops. Its layout includes buildings that archaeologist Mark Merrony says are consistent with a headquarters and a commander’s house. The finds support the presence of a Roman military site; whether Magnus Maximus himself was there remains unproven.

content.headline: Optogenetic gene therapy restores some vision in six of 10 patients
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy restores some vision in six patients
content.standfirst: A small trial used a gene therapy and amber-light glasses to help some people with retinitis pigmentosa detect objects. The result is an early advance, not a cure or a return to normal vision.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control the activity of nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: A gene therapy that makes retinal nerve cells respond to amber light improved vision in six of 10 people with severe retinitis pigmentosa in a study reported in The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants wore special glasses that convert ordinary light into amber shades and needed weeks of training to interpret what they saw.

segments.title: An early step, with wider possibilities still unproven
segments.body: The reported gains included tasks such as picking up a cup; patients could not distinguish between faces. Optogenetics uses light to activate or quiet nerve cells, and researchers are exploring possible applications for pain, epilepsy and hearing. The hearing work remains at the animal-testing stage, and gene therapies may be irreversible, so safety and further clinical testing remain central questions.

content.headline: Women with autoimmune disease report more psychological misdiagnoses
content.shortHeadline: Women report more psychological misdiagnoses for autoimmune disease
content.standfirst: A study of more than 6,600 people found women more often reported psychiatric or psychosomatic explanations for autoimmune symptoms and longer waits for diagnosis. Its findings highlight reported experiences, not proof of why each delay occurred.

image.caption: Autoimmune thyroid disease was among the conditions reported by participants in the study.

sources.originalTitle: Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’

segments.body: In a study involving more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions, 43% of women said they had been told their condition had a psychiatric cause, compared with 33% of men. Women were also more likely to report that symptoms had been labelled psychosomatic and to describe longer waits between symptoms beginning and diagnosis.

segments.title: What the study can—and cannot—show
segments.body: After adjusting for factors including age, disease group, continent and household finances, the researchers reported that women were 46% more likely than men to report a psychiatric misdiagnosis and 74% more likely to report a psychosomatic one. Most participants were women and from the UK, and the results are based on patient reports. The authors say complex, often invisible symptoms challenge diagnosis for everyone, while women may face additional disadvantages.

content.headline: Climate change is prompting research into crops suited to hotter, drier Britain
content.shortHeadline: Researchers test crops for a hotter, drier Britain
content.standfirst: Researchers and farmers are testing drought-tolerant crops such as lupins and chickpeas as hot, dry summers hit familiar harvests. Which varieties can thrive in Britain—and where—still needs to be established.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from a crop being explored for warmer, drier conditions.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: After a hot, dry summer damaged yields of familiar crops, a government-funded research network is investigating alternatives that may cope better with warmer, drier conditions. Researchers at the University of Southampton are studying crops including lupins and chickpeas, while working with food businesses and chefs on ways to use them.

segments.title: Testing before planting at scale
segments.body: Lupins are drought-tolerant and their beans can be processed into flour; chickpeas are also being explored as a potential British crop. But researchers say more work is needed to establish where varieties grow best and to understand risks from pests and disease. Experts also caution that a warmer climate will not make every crop suitable everywhere: late spring frosts can still damage fruit-tree blossom.

content.headline: Cyril Hilsum, physicist whose research helped bring liquid-crystal screens to TV
content.shortHeadline: Cyril Hilsum’s research helped bring liquid-crystal screens to life
content.standfirst: Hilsum led work on stable liquid crystals for radar displays that later helped make flat-panel screens practical. His research also spanned semiconductors, infrared lasers and microwave technology.

image.caption: Cyril Hilsum at GEC’s research centre in Wembley in 1983.

sources.originalTitle: Cyril Hilsum obituary

segments.body: Cyril Hilsum, who has died aged 101, led a Ministry of Defence team in the late 1960s tasked with developing flat displays for miniature radar systems. Working with George Gray and Peter Raynes, his team developed a stable liquid-crystal mixture by 1972, helping make durable liquid-crystal displays practical.

segments.title: Research with a lasting reach
segments.body: The displays were later used in products including watches, calculators, laptops, tablets and phones. Hilsum’s work also included semiconductor research, infrared lasers that underpin fibre-optic telecommunications, and the Gunn diode, used to generate microwave signals. He later became the UK’s chief scientific officer and advocated for women in science during his leadership at GEC.

content.headline: Researchers trace spyware attacks to online ads, revealing a route for covertly
content.shortHeadline: Researchers trace spyware attacks to online ads
content.standfirst: Researchers say a platform linked to an Israeli ad firm enabled spyware to target devices through ordinary-looking ads, without a click. They found evidence of infections at Al Jazeera, but the full extent and the governments behind the attacks remain unknown.

sources.originalTitle: Online ads weaponised to deliver ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers say
An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
Citizen Lab says governments are abusing online ads to hack people with ‘zero-click’ spyware

segments.body: Researchers at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab say Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising firm, operated a platform called Controlium that helped spyware makers target devices through online ads. The researchers say the attacks needed no click or other action from the user. They found evidence that at least 45 Windows computers at Al Jazeera were infected in 2024 and 2025.

segments.title: A wider advertising risk
segments.body: Citizen Lab says exposed records showed ads appearing across thousands of apps and websites, including on devices used by government and critical-infrastructure networks. That does not establish that those devices were infected, and the researchers say they do not know which governments were behind the attacks. The findings point to risks in ad systems that use user and device profiles to place adverts.

perspectives.body: The Verge reports that Google and ad platform Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from their platforms, while IAB Europe suspended the firm from its approved-vendor list. Researchers also advised people at higher risk of targeting to use ad blockers and disable ad tracking.

content.headline: AI-linked tech shares fall as inflation fears deepen investor doubts
content.shortHeadline: AI-linked shares slide as inflation and spending fears mount
content.standfirst: A sell-off hit chipmakers and technology-heavy markets after US inflation data raised the prospect of higher interest rates. Investor concern about the scale of AI investment is adding pressure, but the reports do not establish that the sector’s outlook has fundamentally changed.

image.caption: A market display shows South Korea’s Kospi index after a sharp fall in technology shares.

sources.originalTitle: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt

segments.body: Shares in major technology and chip companies fell across the US and Asia after US inflation data came in higher than expected. South Korea’s Kospi 200 dropped 8.1%, triggering trading halts; Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 4.9%. Samsung and SK Hynix were among the sharp fallers, while the Nasdaq also declined.

segments.title: Two sources of market anxiety
segments.body: Investors are weighing the possibility that higher inflation could lead the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, making borrowing more expensive. At the same time, markets are questioning the scale and financing of AI investment. The International Monetary Fund has warned that an AI share-price correction could affect global financial stability, though the scale of any risk remains uncertain.

content.headline: New data-centre plans in Norfolk and Scotland face questions over land and jobs
content.shortHeadline: Data-centre plans raise questions over land, power and jobs
content.standfirst: A proposed Norfolk data centre would need up to 1GW of power, alongside a large solar farm; a separate Scottish plan promises jobs at a former nuclear site. Both remain proposals, with questions about local impacts and the benefits for communities.

sources.originalTitle: Huge data centre and solar farm plans revealed
Outlander star criticises data centre plan for nuclear site

segments.body: Developers Evolution Power Limited say a proposed Norfolk data centre could require up to 1 gigawatt of electricity, alongside a solar farm designed to generate up to 1.3GW. The two sites would cover about 4,695 acres, and the company says the project could attract £25bn in investment and create more than 500 permanent roles. It expects to submit a planning application next April.

segments.title: Local benefits under debate
segments.body: A separate data-centre proposal at Chapelcross, a former nuclear site in Dumfries and Galloway, has drawn criticism from actor Sam Heughan, who questioned its long-term jobs and environmental impact. The developer says the scheme could provide about 540 operational jobs, with up to 750 during construction. Scottish ministers say national guidance on data-centre planning is due by Christmas; neither proposal has been approved.

perspectives.body: Heughan called for a pause on large data-centre proposals, arguing that economic gains could flow mainly to US technology companies while the sites affect local landscapes and wildlife. The developer presents Chapelcross as a route to renewable energy, digital infrastructure and jobs.

content.headline: Flock chief says microphones detect only gunshots, while its website lists more
content.shortHeadline: Flock’s microphone claims clash with its website
content.standfirst: Flock’s chief executive said the company’s microphones listen for “just gunshots”. Its site also describes detection of fireworks, sideshows and crashes, while the company says the system is not designed to monitor conversations or identify distress.

sources.originalTitle: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different

segments.body: Flock CEO Garrett Langley defended the company’s Gunshot Detection system at a public event, saying it detects “just gunshots”. But the company’s website says its audio technology can also detect fireworks, sideshows and car crashes, and that its detection library is expanding. The contrast has drawn scrutiny as communities debate the reach of surveillance systems.

segments.title: What the company says it detects
segments.body: Flock said its system is primarily used to detect gunfire and can identify some other sounds, but is not designed to monitor conversations or analyse speech. The company said it no longer offers detection of human screaming or distress. Its microphones and other surveillance products face growing criticism from privacy advocates and members of the public.

content.headline: Researcher says AI toy exposed millions of conversations and children’s profiles
content.shortHeadline: AI toy security flaw exposed conversations, researcher says
